newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Former HK prosecutor jailed for 2-1/2 years in NZ.
newsitem.headline: Former HK prosecutor jailed for 2-1/2 years in NZ.

text.p: A New Zealand court on Wednesday sentenced a disgraced former Hong Kong prosecutor to two and a half years in jail for accepting a NZ$1 million (US$700,000) bribe.

Warwick Reid, 48, had pleaded guilty to a charge of wilfully attempting to pervert the course of justice. The verdict effectively scotched the possibility of his extradition to Hong Kong to face further corruption charges there.

A High Court judge in the North Island city of Rotorua said he would have sentenced Reid to four years, but reduced the jail term in the light of his guilty plea and the fact that he had spent two months in prison on remand.
Reid was deported to New Zealand in November 1994 after serving four years and eight months in a Hong Kong jail for taking bribes as a senior Crown prosecutor to fix corruption trials.
The New Zealander, who admitted accepting HK$12.4 million in bribes, had his original eight-year sentence reduced in return for testifying against his accomplices.
Earlier this year, he was arrested by New Zealand police for perjury in an affidavit he made in support of an appeal by a Hong Kong businessman, Ch'ng Poh, against a fraud conviction.
The affidavit was signed shortly after Reid's 1994 deportation.

Hong Kong's Independent Commission Against Corruption had been seeking Reid's extradition to face charges including conspiracy to commit perjury, using a false affidavit and conspiring to pervert the course of justice.
Friends of Reid have said he pleaded guilty to the charges in New Zealand because he feared retribution from his enemies if he went back to Hong Kong.

According to press reports, Reid spent time in a psychiatric hospital earlier this year after atempting to commit suicide. He appeared relaxed at Wednesday's hearing, where he declined an invitation by the judge to comment.
In a television interview recorded earlier this year and screened on Wednesday, he said his life would be in danger, even in prison, if he returned to Hong Kong.
"Nightmares of solitary confinement will never leave me. I always have flashbacks in relation to those times," he said of his Hong Kong jail term.
Even in New Zealand, Reid said, he was still looking over his shoulder for possible threats to his life. "I'm not totally oblivious to the risks. I've still got a long way to go."
